new_items.title: A shared interbacterial membrane underlies mycobacterial cording.
new_items.summary_rss: Virulent mycobacteria grow into mechanically resilient serpentine cords, yet how individual cells coordinate growth, division, and adhesion to form cords remains unknown. Here, combining live-cell fluorescence microscopy with cryo-electron tomography, we show that snapping division generates a shared interbacterial membrane (IBM) between daughter cells, in which each bacterium contributes one leaflet continuous with the inner leaflet of the mycomembrane. During cord formation, the IBM extends laterally as the daughter cells align along a common axis, restricting the outer mycomembrane leaflet largely to the exterior. The increased IBM interleaflet spacing is consistent with the retention of trehalose mycolates in both leaflets. In Mycobacterium tuberculosis, an interleaflet density is associated with the secretion of phthiocerol dimycocerosate and ESX-1 substrates. Our results reveal a multi-bacterial membrane architecture that provides the structural basis for cording and for collective behaviors, including mechanical stability, molecular exchange, phage resistance, and the sequestration of surface-associated virulence factors within the cord interior.

new_items.title: Cardiomyocyte-derived circulating extracellular vesicles enable a non-invasive liquid biopsy of human myocardium.
new_items.summary_rss: Non-invasive interrogation of difficult-to-sample tissues remains a central challenge in human health. Here, we identify and characterize cardiomyocyte-derived extracellular vesicles (EVs; "cardiovesicles") as a liquid interface to the myocardium. Integrating induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes, genetic models, and multi-omics, we identify two cardiomyocyte-enriched surface markers (POPDC2 and CHRNE), enabling antibody-based cardiovesicle immunocapture from human plasma. Cardiovesicles are enriched for cardiomyocyte transcripts, exhibiting disease-specific transcriptional signatures in heart failure and myocardial infarction. Paired human myocardial tissue-plasma analyses demonstrate cardiac enrichment (versus bulk EVs) and concordance with myocardial single-nucleus transcriptional profiles. In patients undergoing cardiopulmonary bypass, cardiovesicles capture rapid, dynamic transcriptional changes that parallel cardiomyocyte (not fibroblast, endothelial, and myeloid) responses to ischemic stress. Functional genomics implicates cardiovesicle transcripts in cardiomyocyte cell-specific cardiovascular disease liability in large human populations. Cardiovesicles may capture dynamic cardiomyocyte states in humans that reflect genetic disease liability, supporting an EV-based approach to non-invasive liquid biopsy of the myocardium.
